title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with a synthetic likeness, not a model error inside a business system. A caller on a WhatsApp video call presented himself as a sitting chief minister, and the fabrication was convincing enough in voice and appearance to sustain a conversation about financial aid. The same channel then carried further impersonations, a person claiming to be the minister's manager and later a person claiming to be a CBI officer, each one adding a new demand for money.

The failure sits at the point of contact between a member of the public and an unauthenticated caller. Nothing in the call itself let the recipient test whether the face and voice belonged to the person claimed, and no step in the sequence required the claimed identities to be confirmed through any channel outside the fraudsters' own. Catching it would have taken verification of the caller through an independent, official route before any payment, because the deepfake was built precisely to survive the judgement a recipient would normally make from seeing and hearing a familiar public figure.

What is not established is who made the deepfake, who placed the calls, or whether anyone will be found responsible. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act, which is an allegation recorded by police and not a finding of guilt. The account of the payments rests on a single outlet's report, and the description of this as the city's first reported case of its kind is that report's characterisation.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, aged 29 and originally from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9. The caller used an AI deepfake to appear and sound like Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and offered Rs 11 lakh in financial aid. A person posing as Vijay's manager said Rs 5 lakh had been allotted and asked Giri to pay charges. This was the city's first reported case of its kind.

Giri was first asked for Rs 5,000 as exchange charges, then Rs 18,000 to unlock his PIN. A fake CBI officer named Thakur later demanded over Rs 50,000 as a fine. Fearing he would lose earlier payments, Giri transferred money and made more payments totaling over Rs 1.04 lakh. When the fraudsters asked for another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he had been duped. He contacted the cybercrime helpline 1930 and then Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act. Police advised people not to trust such calls or make payments based on them.
title_en: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh
